Sarthak Ahuja on Instagram: "If you have a bank loan currently, you immediately need to take this one step as your next EMI is going to be higher...

The RBI increased the repo rate from 5.25% to 5.5%, which means by 0.25%....

So if your floating home loan was earlier at 7.5%... it will now be at 7.75%...

This means, you either have the choice to increase your EMI outflow per month to keep the same tenure, or increase the tenure to keep the EMI the same...

Most banks will silently increase your tenure... because they make more money by doing it...

I’ll explain the math...

Imagine you had a loan of Rs 1 crore for 20 years at 7.5%... your EMI would be Rs ~80,559/-... and you would pay a total interest of Rs 93 lakh on your loan...

When the rate changes to 7.75% and the duration continues to be 20 years, your EMI goes up by only Rs 1500 per month, and your total interest payout is Rs 97 lakhs...

But if you keep your EMI the same to Rs ~80,500 and increase duration to 1 year...

you end up paying an interest of Rs ~1,03,000/-... almost Rs 6 lakhs higher.

So take the option of paying Rs 1500 extra as EMI per month instead of increasing the tenure.

#casarthakahuja"

1️⃣ Easy to undo, nobody notices: let it handle it (archiving newsletters, declining cold pitches)
2️⃣ Easy to undo, but it goes out in your name: have it draft and wait for your yes (client replies, anything that books your time)
3️⃣ Hard to undo: have it bring it straight to you (money, legal, anyone you know personally)

Mark Manson on Instagram: "In 2018, a team of psychologists at Harvard ran one of the simplest experiments I’ve ever read about, and I still think about it all the time.

They sat people in front of a screen and showed them dots, one at a time. Some dots were blue. Some were purple. The job was easy. Look at the dot and say whether it’s blue.

At first, everyone did fine. Then the researchers slowly cut back on the blue dots, and people started calling purple dots blue. Their brains were running low on blue, so they stretched the definition until they had enough of it again.

The researchers didn’t stop at dots. They tried faces, and as the threatening faces got rarer, people started reading neutral faces as threatening. They tried research proposals, and as the unethical ones got rarer, perfectly harmless proposals started looking shady.

They even warned some of the participants that this would happen. They offered others cash to stay consistent. The drift showed up anyway.

The paper calls it “prevalence-induced concept change.” I call it the Blue Dot Effect, because nobody is going to remember “prevalence-induced concept change” at a dinner party.

Now think about the biggest problem in your life five years ago. Maybe it was money. Maybe you were lonely, or stuck in a job that made you want to drive into a lake every Monday morning.

There’s a decent chance you fixed it, or at least got a lot closer. And there’s a very good chance you don’t feel five years’ worth of better. A new problem moved into the spot the old one left. It’s probably smaller. It sure doesn’t feel smaller.

That’s the blue dot. Your mind keeps a certain amount of worry on file, and when one worry leaves, it goes shopping for a replacement."

Kneel on one knee with the other foot positioned in front of you. Both knees should be at approximately 90°.

Obviously, here I’m talking about career success (but there are parallels to this in other areas of life). 

Also obvious is that we can’t always do the work that we would like to do most. There are practical considerations. 

But ultimately, if we want to make a living doing what we love most and do our very best work, it’s important we invest time in what we are most interested in seeing in the world and curious about.

This clip excerpt is from me as a guest on the podcast Invest With the Best. 

He asked me: “what is the kindest thing anyone has ever done for you?”

My answer was that Barbara Chapman, who eventually became my PhD advisor, had reminded me that the most important thing is to work on the things we are most curious about. And ignore any internal or external noise about what we should be doing instead.

Barbara and I went onto publish a lot of studies together. It was a ton of work, but we had so much fun doing those projects. In no small part because I was trying to answer the questions about the brain and brain development that were most burning for me at the time. 

Some years later, I shifted to working on other scientific questions (postdoc years) and then again (before tenure) and again (after tenure) and I eventually launched the Huberman Lab podcast. 

Because that’s where my curiosity went. Each stage worked out great. And there will be a next stage of interests at some point too. 

None of it came easy, but I’m so glad Barbara convinced me to follow my curiosity. Always. 

The takeaway is that whether field or career track is crowded or empty, if you follow your strongest curiosity, your motivation never flags (if you take care of yourself physically that is!) and you inevitably do your best work.

So once again, while there are practical considerations along one’s life and career track, when you can, follow your curiosity, even if it means going against the grain. 

I did. And I never looked back. And I’ll continue to do that going forward. 

My wish for everyone - for you, is that you do the same."

NRI Shaala by Aspora on Instagram: "Your OCI Card Doesn’t Give You These Rights 

Getting an OCI card can feel like becoming Indian again.
You can live in India indefinitely, work and study here, and buy most types of property without applying for a new visa every time you enter the country. But there’s an important line many OCI holders misunderstand:
OCI is not Indian citizenship.

That means no voting rights, no contesting elections, no regular government jobs and restrictions still apply to purchasing agricultural land and farmland.

So while an OCI card gives you significant rights to live and build a life in India, it doesn’t give you every right an Indian citizen has.

Think of it this way:

OCI gives you “live here freely.”
Citizenship gives you “belong here legally as a citizen.”
Know the difference before you assume your OCI card covers everything.
